utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I take it that the Defence is ready to continue the examination of the witness. Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness, Mr. Gray, into the courtroom. I'd like to use the time meanwhile to indicate to the parties that we cannot start tomorrow at 2.15 since there is an initial appearance in the same courtroom. The parties should keep themselves available to start with the hearing on from 3.15 tomorrow. So it might be that we are never sure how much time an initial appearance will take so it might be that we cannot immediately start at 3.15 but the parties should keep themselves available. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the registrar informs me that there has been -- you used one hour yesterday for the witness, Mr. Gray, and your estimate -- time estimate was -- I haven't got it clearly in my mind at this very moment but it is certainly written down somewhere. Four hours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gray. We're a bit delayed because the morning session took a bit more time than we expected, therefore we'll start a bit later than we intended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you had given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, good day again.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you first of all tell us very briefly who your command superior was at the time of the events?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: My -- at which point in time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, if there was -- if you had several superiors while you were there, tell us their names, please. Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes. My immediate superior was Colonel John B. Wilson. He was later a brigadier. He was a chief military observer. When sector Sarajevo was created, the commander was General Lewis McKenzie. The overall commander was Lieutenant Colonel Satish Nambiar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to talk about the second officer you mentioned, about General MacKenzie. Could you please tell us what kind of relations you had with him and I mean purely personal relations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: We had very strong, good personal relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, I'd like to show an exhibit, 1846, I think -- I hope that's the right number. Thank you. It's a document dated the 29th of July, 1992. I see we only have one page here, I don't know why, but -- I'm sorry about this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's true, this is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, wait a minute, please. Do you recognise the letter? Have you already seen it somewhere?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd be grateful if you could read item three in this letter, could you do so, please? Could you read it out aloud? Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Gray --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We can read what's on the piece of paper. It is inappropriate to lead this sort of evidence from a witness in chief bolstering character. The witness is not under attack in relation to his character. It is self-serving in that sense and it is also clearly distressing to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't want to disturb anyone and certainly not the Prosecution, but we have heard many things in the witness' absence. We have a document here and I think we could hear it being read out allowed. I don't know if we should tender a document which I don't even know if it's going to be accepted later but not yet, just a minute, Mr. Ierace, I'd like to finish. Mr. President, I'd like to finish. Thank you. It's of great importance for the credibility of this witness. We should learn not only what we might think about it but what might great professionals might have thought about him at the time of the events and this is information that should be rendered public. It's necessary to read it given that we don't know what the attitude of the Prosecution will be at the end of the hearing with regard to accepting or rejecting such a document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, nothing was said contradictory to what was said in paragraph 3 in front of us. It was inappropriate for my learned colleague to say that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, there is no reason not to hear about the credentials of this witness in a public hearing, but since it seems to evoke some emotions with him, the Chamber suggests that you read the parts you want to draw our attention to and ask the witness about -- the questions you have in mind. So -- but you asked him already, you started already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can read it out. I can read it out. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you please read paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Paragraph 3, Lieutenant Colonel Gray demonstrated great personal courage."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but it's certain -- raises some emotions with you. I will read it. "Paragraph 3 which is Lieutenant Colonel Gray demonstrated great personal courage on numerous occasions. He was always first a volunteer for risky missions and he naturally led by example." If there's any other part please read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'll read the last page. I apologise, the last line under item four which interests us because of the following questions, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: "Progress to date on the airport agreement owes a good deal to his efforts."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This brings me, witness, to item four. As far as you can remember, what can you tell us about the efforts you made to obtain an agreement on the airport, first of all?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay, I did all the planning for the opening of the airport, all of them in this document here. Which reads: "Planning consideration to verify the withdrawal of all arms weapons and locate the location and direction of --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, witness, I apologise. We'll present this document in a minute. We'll tender it so it's not necessary to read it. We are simply interested in what you can remember. Could you briefly tell us what you did within the framework of the so-called airport agreement? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I did all the planning for the opening of the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What did that involve, Colonel Gray, or what was involved when you spoke about the opening of the airport?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was a military exercise, intellectual exercise on my behalf in order to provide the headquarters of UNPROFOR with the detail that I considered necessary in order to open the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, what was the objective of opening the airport, why was it necessary to open it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The airport was required to be opened because people were short of food and basic items to live, and so the Serbs agreed, after the airport agreement, to actually let the airport be taken over by the UN in order to bring in the humanitarian aid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned about the Serbian desire to allow the airport to be opened. What can you tell us about the willingness of the other party or of the other parties, if we're talking both about the Croats and the Muslims at that time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They had very little say about it because they didn't control the airport. I mean, the Serbs controlled the airport and they willingly gave that over to the UN in order to allow humanitarian aid to be delivered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, with the assistance of the usher and the leave of Mr. President, I'm going to show you a document, the number it bears is 1847. Here it is. And the question I want to put to you is as follows: Could you have a quick look at the document and tell us whether it's a document that you mentioned a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, it is, I wrote it. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you confirm that it was signed by yourself? I think I can see your signature at the bottom; is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by the person who is mentioned below you, that is to say, Dr. -- above, not below, Dr. Nikola Koljevic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yeah, a very nice person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We can put this document aside, witness. Colonel, I'd like you to tell us whether you were informed about a second agreement between the sides that you might have been involved in and if there was such a second agreement, what was concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. This is the main, main thing. This is the main point of contention, I think. When General Lewis MacKenzie left Sarajevo in July, a vacuum was created. There was only a chief of staff, a French Colonel, Davout, a very nice person but he was a chief of staff. I have been a chief of staff for a formation, a brigade headquarters in a large, large formation of thousands of soldiers. A chief of staff has the primary function to run the headquarters and follow the commander's intent or his orders. In the absence of a commander and therefore no intent, no direction, nothing was happening. A war was just going on. I, as a senior military observer in Sarajevo was aware, through my military observers, about -- I mean they were spread around Sarajevo. We were aware of heavy weapons which were not under UN observation. I, therefore, of my own initiative, undertook to create a second agreement for the concentration of heavy weapons. I did this and I concluded this with Serbs firstly, and then with the Presidency side or the Muslim side. They both signed the agreement. General Galic was a party to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. With the leave of Mr. President, I suggest that we show you Exhibit D109, D for Defence and naturally with the assistance of Madam Registrar, who is going to find it for us. We have copies here, but we need to find the original document. The document in question is D109. And Witness, when you are shown this document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have D109A and we have D109B.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well let's start by one or the other. We think it's the same document. Let's start with A. Usher, I would be grateful if you could hand all this out. Thank you. And perhaps to put --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, have you had the time to have a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this document conform to what you just pointed out to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I wrote the document. It's mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that on page 3, your signature is indicated; did you also sign the document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you also confirm that Mr. Radovan Karadzic signed this document?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: This document was signed by Radovan Karadzic and it was also signed by Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, in relation to this agreement, reached with regard to heavy weapons, I would now like to focus on a certain issue. The first question is: At this time when this agreement was signed, did the Serb forces give you access or did -- or perhaps did they prevent you from having access to their heavy weapons?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say no, what do you mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They did not prevent us from having access. They willingly showed us where there were extra locations where they had heavy weapons which were not under UN supervision and they willingly did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But did you have the possibility, when counting shots, to come across information, to compare the information that the Serb side gave you with observations made by UN observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever come to the conclusion that your UN observations contradicted those presented to you by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to go back to the issue of the spirit of the agreements. As far as the spirit of the agreements is concerned, if you are able to judge this yourself, what could you tell us about the spirit that moved the Serbian side at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Serbian side at the time were -- I mean they wanted a political solution to the whole war and that was exhibited by the fact that the Serbian side always signed the agreements first and the Presidency side always signed them second. And the Presidency side were forced, I mean at some great length, to actually sign the agreements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the Serbs seeking in the spirit, could you tell us in a couple of words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They wanted their own self-determination. They wanted to keep the territory that they had always held and that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you under the impression, given the situation on the ground, that the territory that they said was theirs and the actual situation, reality, did you have the impression that these two factors corresponded to each other. I will withdraw that question. I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to leading by my friend in formulating his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes it's better to prevent the situation to exist but since the question is withdrawn, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would now like to examine the situation from a different perspective, that is to say, the perspective of the so-called Muslim side. As far as the spirit of the agreements is concerned, and in particular, the spirit of the agreement that we are talking about now, what, in your opinion, was the position of the so-called Muslim army?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, they -- they objected strenuously and it was extremely hard to get their agreement, I mean their signature on the agreement. It was very, very difficult. I went to a meeting with Lieutenant General Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Satish Nambiar and Alija Izetbegovic was there and Stjepan Kljujic was there. We had -- Mr. Halilovic was there. All the key players, Stjepan Siber was there, they were all at this meeting and I had been trying for days and days to get this agreement signed and it was virtually impossible. I had Satish Nambiar sitting on my right-hand side and I pushed Mr. Izetbegovic or President Izetbegovic, I pushed him so hard about signing this agreement that Satish Nambiar actually took out his left hand and grabbed my right hand and he nearly broke my fingers squeezing them so hard to stop me pushing Izetbegovic about this agreement. Two days later, the Presidency side signed it. That was the amount of resistance there was about having peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, why was there, as you said, why was there a resistance to find peace or rather to achieve peace?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Serbian forces were basically -- in Bosnia wanted to keep the land that they had for a long time, hundreds of years. The Muslims, on the other hand, or the Presidency side, wanted to totally cleanse Bosnia and Herzegovina of any Serbians and have a totally Muslim state. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us to change the topic now and if we can now look at the opening of fire. I am speaking of artillery now or about weapons like rocket launchers.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather not rocket launchers, mortars, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel. Here was an enemy. If you were being fired at, is it legitimate to return fire? As far as you know about military profession, is that legitimate?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Of course it is. It has to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let us focus on the firing that was coming from the city. Yesterday, you spoke to us about vehicles that were carrying mortars on them and you told us that there was fire opened towards the Serb forces from these weapons. Now, my question is the following: This technique that was used, did they seem to you to be something that was done rarely, exceptionally or rather this was something that this was provocation technique done in a systematic manner?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: This was absolutely routine. It was routine. It was routine. They drove these vehicles around Sarajevo. They would fire one mortar bomb and then they would move so that when the counter-battery fire came back, there would be no one there apart from, unfortunately, civilians. But I mean this was quite deliberate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you speak of routine. If I ask you to qualify or quantify this routine in terms of time, in terms of frequency, was this something that happened once a week, once a month, ten times a period of time, I don't know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It depended on the amount of ammunition that they had and I mean we can deal with that point later. But I mean it really depended on the amount of ammunition that they had. I mean the artillery position that was up by the tower, the TV tower, up there, that artillery position with 105 Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we please have it on the ELMO so we can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Where's the pointer? Okay. The TV tower is there, okay, that's where --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment. Just a moment, Colonel. First I have to describe for the transcript what you are showing. For the transcript, the witness is pointing to a hill called Hum. Could you please continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the witness does continue I'm having some trouble with my screen. Could I have some assistance, perhaps from one of the technicians while the witness gives his evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we now have a look again, the image on the screen that I had and could you please point again?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: This is the position of the TV tower. This is where I had observers monitoring 105 millimetre Howitzers. The only inability of the Presidency side to actually use these howitzers what that that they'd run out of ammunition but they were remanufacturing ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll talk about it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in order to avoid whatever confusion, the map the witness is using at this very moment is not the map he used yesterday and he marked yesterday. If you'd -- either we have to identify what map he's using or present to him the map we used yesterday. Perhaps the latter is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It may be that this is the witness', originally it was the same map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore either identify that map or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, witness, please, could you do the following? Take this map from the ELMO and what we are going to do is going to place a different map on the ELMO with the assistance of Madam Registrar and the map in question is exactly the same map as the previous one and I will ask you to point again so that we can be sure that we are talking about the same thing. Not with a pen, please. With the pointer, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, this is the wrong one. It's further.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, you're right, which shows us this is what we need is the second part of the map, the second half of the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's one map consisting of two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Colonel, for your observation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness made some marking on the map that was presented to him yesterday especially on the eastern part where he marked numbers 4, 5, 7, 8. Yes, that's the one. Perhaps he could use that one. Yes, but it was in two parts, an eastern part and a western part. I think as a matter of fact, that yes, -- if we are talking about Hum hill that's on the eastern part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I would be grateful if you can look at number 4 or 5. That will be -- no, no, more to -- no, no, more to -- more to the west, please. Yes. What number do you have, that's a number 6, I believe? Yes. Are we now speaking of the same thing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the witness has identified number 6 which is just above Novo Sarajevo and I believe that there is the name of Hum there. Very well, now, witness, let us go back to the question of mobile mortars and of the frequency of their firing. You said that this depended but according to your personal experience, what I want to know is whether this was something that happened several times a week, several times a month or several times a day and so on. If you can tell us something about that, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Several times a day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your earlier answer, Witness, you said that the -- this caused killing of civilians. Do you think that this was part of a strategy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to leading. I would be grateful if my friend would not lead the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What can you tell us about this topic in terms of a strategy? Mr. President, just one thing, if I am mistaken, this is just by error and of course Mr. Ierace will stand up and will let me know if he can. I will rephrase my question. Witness, what can you tell us in relation to the firing, if you know about the purpose of this firing, if you know anything about that. We're not speaking with the frequency.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. There was a -- in my view, a definite strategy to deliberately provoke --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, by his questions, has led the witness by invitation to offer theories. He has not made clear in his questions any distinction between known facts and opinion. This is similar to an objection I made yesterday and in my respectful submission, it is appropriate to elicit what the witness knows quite separate from what opinions the witness might have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we are faced with a problem that you did lead the witness and then of course if you withdraw the question and then put a question in the similar area then the effect of leading has not been undone. Would you please move for this moment to your next subject and you will certainly find a suitable moment to ask the witness about facts that might finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President, I will do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, you told us yesterday -- you told us about a scene, the scene was about the arrival of a politician to Sarajevo; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe, and I'm speaking from memory, you used the term of murder. You spoke of murder.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you now tell us only about the fact, do you know, do you have any knowledge about facts that you can relate to the things that you have known that have taken place in Sarajevo and if you do, can you tell us about them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please do that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. We had a number of politicians who came to Sarajevo including President Mitterand, Lord Carrington and there are a number of other politicians who came in to try and resolve the whole situation. Each time they arrived, there were two separate programmes. They had meetings with the Serb side, normally at the airport. Some of them, I think, were at Lukavica, but mostly at the airport, and we actually sent UN armoured personnel carriers to Lukavica to uplift the Serb politicians and bring them to the airport so that they were protected and they could have their meeting. Then, there were the other meetings which were held at the Presidency, always at the Presidency. The two programmes for the meetings were always only told to the separate sides. Neither side got a total copy of the programme. It -- it became predictable that whenever any politician went to the Presidency, and this was without the knowledge of the Serbs, they didn't know the precise timing, that mortar bombs would land immediately outside the Presidency and would kill or wound people. Media, media coverage, of course, was always there in terms of the BBC, and CNN because they knew that Lord Carrington or whoever was going to actually be at a meeting in the Presidency and it was a big media thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Thank you, Colonel. You're telling us about shelling and my question is the following: Did you have an opportunity in your career to see a number of mortar craters; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see many? I'm not asking you to give us a precise figure, but an approximation, more than ten, more than 50, more than 100?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I did a mortar course. I mean I -- I mean I did a heavy weapons course in which I learned how to actually use mortars and during my time in Sarajevo, I saw many mortar craters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us if you have ever seen, you personally, and I'm only speaking exclusively about mortars, so have you ever seen a situation -- no, I withdraw that. I will withdraw that so that I don't provoke any problems. I will rephrase my question. Could you please describe to the Chamber what does a mortar crater look like that we see, that we can find on hard surfaces, for instance, on asphalt?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. When a mortar bomb lands, whether it's a -- the people in Sarajevo on either side, they were only using 82-millimetre mortars or 120-millimetre mortars. When a mortar bomb lands, it leaves a very nice neat little -- it's a very small crater. I should have brought some photos. And there is a completely uniform splatter mark from the shrapnel that comes out from the actual mortar impact and the mortar, the tail fin is never destroyed, it will break off on impact and it will be a short distance away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, in your experience, what is the depth of such a crater on an asphalt surface, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: On an asphalt surface, the depth would be no more than one centimetre, that's all. That's only -- I mean with -- that's with a super-quick impact. If you use a delayed fuse, it will be deeper and it will create a deeper crater but with super-quick it will just be a centimetre deep, that's all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You're talking about a tail fin, you're speaking about a tail fin that is ejected, gets separated from the shell and then you're telling us about a fuse, that is, you spoke to us of delay fuses and my question is the following: What happens with the stabiliser that is with a tailfin after the explosion when it is used, say hypothetically with a time-delay fuse?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It is still -- I mean they -- the mortar bomb goes into the ground with a delay fuse and that creates a crater. It blows the dirt or whatever out of the crater and therefore the tail fin goes with it. It doesn't stay in the crater. That's it. And normally you find it maybe five metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hypothetical situation where a mortar is found with this kind of time-delay fuse, what does then a crater look like? You said how deep it was but I don't know whether -- it is larger, could you give us a little more information about the nature of such a crater?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the calibre of the mortar. I mean obviously the bigger the mortar, the bigger the crater so if you're using, say, an 82-millimetre mortar, then you would -- with a time-delay fuse, you would expect the crater to be maybe one metre deep, okay. And you'll find the tail fin amongst all the dirt and whatever that's been blown out of the crater, okay. With a 120 millimetre mortar it may be slightly deeper but again, you'll find the tail fin maybe ten metres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm not certain that I heard you correctly. You said one metre in depth, is that what I heard; did I hear this correctly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So if I have one metre in depth, what would be then the diameter, what would be the width, say that the crater is more or less a circle, then what would be the width?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: 1.5 metres. 1.5 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're telling us about a diameter?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Diameter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in none of the two cases, if I understood you correctly, if none of the two cases would the stabiliser tail fin be found inside the crater either in 82 or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Leading, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I answer that? This is not a leading question. The witness said it clearly. I just wanted him to summarise. This was not really a question. It was just asking for a summary. Now, if I understood what the witness said, the witness said that in any case, the stabiliser, the tail fin is ejected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Said that it would be found somewhere next to the crater. In the second answer he said that it would be at a distance of ten metres where the crater would be of a smaller diameter so to that extent it's not leading but was shown in the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President the witness gave his evidence strongly suggesting this is what typically happens and if my learned colleague is willing to explore if there are any exceptions to that typical behaviour with mortar fins, that's what he should have asked. Not to put it in positive terms that in no circumstances does it end up in the crater.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the question to be that in both cases, that is, in both typical situations, whether the situation would be that the tail fin would not end in the crater, not about facts but about typical situations that's how I understood it and both the typical situations being that one would be a fuse that would explode immediately upon impact and the other one the fuse to detonate delayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is not in dispute in terms of typical behaviour. If one then goes to the wording of the question, and we well know the background to the question, then that takes it a step further in positive terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did -- I did not consider the question. I do not think that this witness can tell of his general experience. That's what Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked him about. The answers were clear so I don't know what you are -- please formulate your questions such a way that even an impression of leading would be nonexistent. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. I will be very careful of my questions more and more, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, since we're speaking about craters -- sorry, no, I'll rephrase the question. When there is an artillery -- where there is artillery fire, is there necessarily a crater; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There is normally a crater and it has a very specific marking to it, very specific. It has an impact point and then there is a butterfly effect on the ground which is caused by the shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now speaking as a general rule, not just about mortars but I'm also speaking about artillery fire. Whenever we have artillery fire, is there always a crater, of course if it hits a target or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, there is, and the crater depending on the size of the artillery shell will be bigger or ...

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on this subject, since you are telling us that -- or there's always a crater following artillery fire, has it arrived to you that you have unlike situations under this angle and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question. Has it ever happened to you that you have examined such situations when there was a problem of a crater that is existence or nonexistence of a crater would have posed itself in different terms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, there was. There was a lot of media attention to a casualties at our market and -- in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm not asking you to point at the market. You can just tell us about the fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, the question was whether you had ever -- it ever happened to you that you have examined a specific situation, not what you read or heard in the media but where you examined a situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm very sorry. I had the situation where my observers went, because I sent professional -- I sent an artillery officer and I sent a mortar officer who were totally experienced in knowing what and they were -- they were experienced in doing crater analysis. So they actually knew what they were looking for and that's what I sent them there. And this was the so-called attack on the market where the Serbs were supposed to have actually mortared or shelled at. They found no evidence. No tail fins, they found no -- I mean I can draw you a diagram if you like but I mean when I talked about an artillery shell that lands, it lands and it -- you can tell the direction it comes from because it has a butterfly effect on either side of it, okay. So if it comes from this way the butterfly effect will be from this way and if it comes from this way, the butterfly effect will be this way. And they found nothing. Nothing at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, since you have given us certain elements in your answer, could you locate this incident, could you tell us when it happened and where it happened?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Not precisely. It was a market --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When, first of all?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray. Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Colonel, when, first of all.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was I think in July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you tell us what the name of this place was? What was the object, what was this place?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I honestly can't. I mean it was a market that I had been to personally myself. It was walking distance from the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's perfect. That's sufficient. Thank you. And what happened in this market in terms of casualties, if there were any? What can you tell us about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There were a number of dead and wounded. We or I sent these two officers with another couple of officers to actually go there to examine the scene and find out what they thought had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. You said -- you told us that there were no impact traces, no traces of artillery or mortar impact. What were the conclusions of these experts?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Our conclusions were that it was a bomb. Now who put the bomb there, I don't know, but it was a bomb. There was a crater in the ground and people were killed and wounded, but it wasn't artillery and it wasn't mortar. Who put the bomb there, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you mentioned the media earlier on and that created some confusion. What did you want to say about the media, what could you say about the media in relation to this particular incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The media immediately put a judgement on the -- what had happened and they immediately blamed the Serbs. They had no right to do that. Maybe there was a saboteur from the Serbs who may have placed the bomb there. It certainly wasn't artillery or mortar because there was no evidence to support mortar or artillery fire. The market was placed behind an extremely high building so actually getting the mortar bombs or the artillery there were -- was extremely hard but the media placed an immediate judgement on who had actually done it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Now I have a general question I would like to ask. Can you tell us whether when alleged artillery incidents happened, did one ask for joint commissions to be established after such events, investigation commissions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to go back to the issue of fire. And Mr. President, I'm looking at the time, but perhaps it's the right time to show a video that I should have somewhere in front of me. I'll try to provide the technical booth with it. The number is D34 - and it appears - 8. But we can carry on with other matters for the moment. Witness I'd like to focus on what we call the PTT building now and could you tell us if this was a safe site for UN personnel or was it perhaps a site that was not safe? Why, could you tell us something about your personal experience there, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. It was not safe. We had a number of French soldiers wounded there one evening by 122 shells which came from the Croats, as I found out later. We were shelled a number of times. The people using the 122s on one occasion failed to remove the plug in the front of the shell and actually put a fuse in there so that the shell would actually detonate and so the shell hit the side of the building and it went bump bump bump bump down the actual outside fire escape of the building. We were sniped at many, many times. The Bosnian Presidency actually sent in an anti-sniper team to actually kill their own people who were sniping at us from what I think is a student hostel. No, the PTT was not a safe place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll go back to what you said in a minute. I've taken note of what you said but I would like you to tell us about how frequently the PTT building that you were in was fired at?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: At the very beginning, certainly on the 14th of May and the 8th of June, and then later on, we received a lot of fire but it was not -- it was not frequent. The fact that the Presidency forces decided to park some tanks 50 metres away from the PTT did not assist us whatsoever and these two tanks that were parked there were subsequently destroyed at Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned fire, and when you use this term, when you use the term "fire," you're referring to what we call small arms, SA would be the abbreviation in English or are you referring to some other kind of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to artillery fire, 122, 82 millimetre, 120 millimetre. I mean -- and sniper fire so I mean we -- we were subjected to all sorts of fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, could you tell us, if you know anything about this, of course, could you tell us about the direction or the origin of fire, the origin of fire opened from what we call small arms?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The small arms fire was normally directed from -- actually got -- no. This is the wrong map. We need the other map. The other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with the western part of the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The western part, yeah. Yeah, that's better. Okay. The PTT is here, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness is pointing to the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The fire came from here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wait, please. Thank you. The witness points slightly to the west, to the south-west where there is a crossroads south of the main road and it's a building that is slightly pink. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could we ask the witness to put a mark there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All right, we will do it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please -- witness, just a minute, please. Could you please mark with the following number but I'm not sure whether it's number 9 or number 8, we have to check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it should be 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it number 9? Very well. Could you mark that with number 9, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The ELMO so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The witness marked the site where he said that fire was opened at the PTT building. He marked that site with the number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I think you mentioned a second site, could you please point to this second site?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What is this? What kind of building is this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: This is an apartment building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you mark that site with number 10, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, a minute ago you mentioned something that was the -- called the student's hostel, could you tell us where this student's hostel is located, please? Could you indicate this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. This is the site of number 9. It's number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I can see two buildings there which resemble each other, that is to say, the form is fairly triangular. Have you circled just one of those buildings or both because what you marked seems to -- your mark seems to be on one of these buildings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. No, the fire was coming from both of the buildings. It was both.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, I think it's the right time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we did take a long time because it usually takes some time before the witness so I've asked the usher already to try and find the witness. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In relation to the evidence of Mr. Indic there is a document that I said I would prepare which I now provide copies of, that's P3785 that's the resolution -- the report of the Secretary General. Secondly, last week I said that we wanted identification and copies of the three maps referred to in the Defence shelling expert's report, we still haven't received any correspondence about that and thirdly, yesterday, we were given a CD which the Defence received from the witness said to contain documents and the Defence was having some difficulty accessing the documents. We've managed to open the CD and print off a large number of documents. I've given a bundle to the Defence. There's about 20 or 30 pages still to come I'll provide those at the next break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for this information. I was informed that the diary has been copied and made available to the parties. I hardly dare to ask but is there any progress made in view of the videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I've now viewed all of the videos. If cross-examination commences this evening, or at least if I have an opportunity to ask the witness a few questions, that will assist me in identifying relevant segments to place on to a blank tape to tender tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that you will have an opportunity to put these questions to the witness today. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, are you ready to continue the examination of Mr. Gray?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As always, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, before the break, you mentioned certain features on the map and among them was the so-called students' hostel. My question is as follows: Could you tell us anything about any particular incidents that may have happened and that you might have witnessed from the so-called student hostel building? And could we put the map back on the ELMO as that would assist us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, were you present when any kind of incident occurred with regard to this building while you were in this building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I was. There was two incidents that -- well, there are several incidents but they -- apart from the sniping that was coming from this building to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you. For the English booth, I didn't say while you were in the building, I said in relation to this building. Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: This building was used as part of the front line for the Presidency forces. They were firing towards Nedzarici which is this direction here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, the witness pointed approximately to western or eastern direction in the relation to the boulevard that we can see in the map, please continue.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There was also one incident where -- which I physically saw myself where a yellow Mercedes was trying to escape from Sarajevo towards Ilidza which was held by the Serbs and from this building it was machine-gunned and the people were killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I'd be grateful if you could use the pointer to point at the road where this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is the road which is to the north of the so-called student hostel buildings. Thank you. In what direction did the vehicle go?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The vehicle was travelling to the west and from the PTT here, I was able to physically observe the machine-gun and of the vehicle which happened right there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, I have a question about Alipasino Polje, could you please point to the Alipasino Polje area by using the pointer and could you point to the area between numbers 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The witness complies. Thank you. This area that you pointed to, who -- under whose control was it who had this area under their control as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Presidency and the Muslims had it under their control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, do you know whether on the eastern facades of the buildings of the so-called student hostel buildings, do you know whether there were any firing positions there, any military positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How can you be certain of this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Because they were sniping at us in the PTT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please take a black felt-tip and mark the eastern side of the two buildings, of the two student hostel buildings in order to be sure that we are referring to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I've already marked it as number 9.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I would be grateful if you could mark the eastern side.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are we talking about one building or both buildings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Both buildings, as I said before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So I'm assuming that the eastern side of the second building also contained firing positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, with regard to these firing incidents, and I am only referring to incidents in which small arms were used but I'm also referring to so-called shelling incidents, as a UN official, did you write any protests, did you form any protests? Not necessarily write protests, did you express protests of any kind? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What form did these protests take, written or verbal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Verbal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How did the side to which the protests were addressed react?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Presidency side sent an anti-sniper team to actually kill their own people who were actually firing at us from that particular building. I have it recorded here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, what would be the purpose of sending a team to eliminate one's own men? This seems to be contradictory, what could you tell us with regard to this subject?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It all depends on communication. There was a total lack of communication and that's why the cease-fires never were enduring. I mean that's why you could count -- I could arrange for a cease-fire and it was supposed to come into effect, for example, at 10.00 in the morning and you could count the seconds when the cease-fire was broken because there was a lack of communication. People didn't know there was supposed to be a cease-fire and so they just carried on as usual and the war just carried on. There was no communication -- communication was a major, major problem in this whole conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, earlier on we spoke about the shelling, about -- and in particular about the shelling of a market that was not far from the PTT building and the expression you used was "killed their own people". What did you mean when you said that and could you please expand on that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The coincidence of having international media present when the bomb and we're not talking about mortars or artillery, when the bomb exploded, the coincidence of having media there to immediately get the pictures to the BBC and the CNN was, for us who had been there for months, I mean we had been there for months, was just too incredible to accept. It had to be deliberate in the -- the Lord Carrington visit was absolutely, totally incredible and I can expand on that if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. Please do it.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. When Lord Carrington visited, as I have said before, and the parties, both parties didn't know about the visit programmes of Lord Carrington. Lord Carrington had a meeting, I recall, at the PTT building with the Serbs, it may have been at the airport, it certainly wasn't at Lukavica. He then had a meeting at the Presidency building, he was running late. I went to the Presidency building and I was standing at the front entrance of the Presidency building. Directly opposite me, there was a very nice gentleman. He was 100 metres away from me. I actually have this recorded on videotape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to have to interrupt you. Are you telling us about the same incident that we have already spoken about yesterday or is this a different occasion when the same politician arrived?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, it's probably the same one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise, in this case, I think that I could interrupt you here but what I would like is if we can have a look at something through Madam Registrar, we will have a look at a document B32759. Yes, 32759.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Nine five, the interpreter's correction not five nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the meantime, I'd like to ask the technical booth to be ready to launch the cassette, the very last scene. We will start by the end. This is a night recording but I believe that we found it earlier so this should not pose a problem.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness, when you have the document in front of you, the piece -- when -- the photograph, when it is placed on the ELMO, I'd like you to tell us what you see on it, according to your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There are two photographs, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. This photograph was taken from the Serb side. It is towards the middle of what I would call the middle of Sarajevo. It shows a Holiday Inn and then it shows a building to the right of the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Just a moment. Just a moment. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Identify which photograph is showing to the witness of these two. I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a reference number, 121722A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... A road immediately in front of the photograph, a road and some bushes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. There is a hut. Will you please make the image larger? You see the whole -- zoom out, zoom out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, to the extreme left of the image, we can see a hill and there is a tower on it. Thank you. And the witness points to the tower. Can you please tell us what hill this is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Can I see the map?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, without looking at the map, please, Witness. In relation to the tower which is there, can you tell us is this a facility that you've already spoken about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I said it's where the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you could also have said: Is this -- well, and then -- this is not the way to put the question to the witness. I mean and I really insist now on you refraining from leading Mr. Piletta-Zanin otherwise I'll have to ask you again to move to another subject. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, the centre of the image more or less we can see two buildings, they seem to be higher than the others, taller than the others. Can you please point at them with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness does so. To the left of the first building that you pointed, there is a building which seems to be yellow and brown.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And the witness points to that building. What is this very last building, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What is the building which is right next to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I have no real idea what it was called, but I mean it's this building here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness points at this building. And now, could we please make the building -- image of the building larger so that we can see to one -- [In English] Every detail, okay. To the left. [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, on the facade which is the narrowest of that building, we can see a number of round holes, can you please point at them with the pointer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There's several of them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness does so. According to your experience, to what these holes correspond?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They're from tank rounds.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And they were fired by which side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The facade that you have just indicated, towards which cardinal point is it facing, main point is it facing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It's facing towards the north.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you can -- I'm going to ask you the following question, Witness. You said that the photograph was taken from a Serb position, Serb position. Was it located to the north, south, west or east according to that point of view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, it was from the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, the facade I'm talking to you about which has got tank rounds, which side is it facing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It's facing the south.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got one last question before looking at the video which is coming. If this narrow facade is facing south, logically speaking, then the larger facade which is slightly to the right which key point is it facing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It's facing the east.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to have the cassette shown which we mentioned earlier that is the very last segment on the tape. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, for the technical booth, that was not that segment that I wanted shown but the very last segment, the very, very last segment number nine, bearing number nine which shows us an attack of the building that we just saw. So we would be grateful if we could have a look at that segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There it is, thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we just had a brief look at a scene and I would be grateful to the technical booth if they can prepare this scene for a possible reviewing so that this very last segment -- now, were you able to recognise the building that was located in the middle of the image?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Could you ask the question to the witness because you indicated already when this part was played that we are going about to see a building which we have just been talking about so you have answered that question yourself already. Would you please keep this in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, in relation to this cassette, we saw tracing bullets, tracer bullets. From which side was the attack coming, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was coming from the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can you please take the map, the map that we are working with, and if you can show us, according to your knowledge, the nearest positions in the east in relation to this building? So the nearest Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. The nearest Serb position actually isn't on this map. It's too far to the east.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell us how far were these positions approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Serb positions were several kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, we heard during the -- while we looked at the tape, we saw that -- we heard the noise of the weapons and could you tell us what was the type of the weapons that were used, the noise that you heard, what was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They were medium machine-gun bullets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What diameter, what calibre?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: 7.92 probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why are you saying probably?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, I mean, that was the weapon that the -- well, everyone was using there, 7.92 millimetres and it's a medium machine-gun as opposed to 50 calibre or a 12 millimetre or a 14.5 millimetre which are classed as heavy machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In this attack that you saw, could it have been a weapon of a larger calibre than the one that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why not? Why definitely not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Because the sound is wrong. I know this -- I know the sound of a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But is there something in relation to the rhythm or anything in particular that you can indicate to us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It is. The actual rate of fire is far too high for a heavy machine-gun. The firing is going far too fast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. To the extent that this is a 12.7 or 12.9 calibre -- what is the calibre that was used?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. To the extent that this is a 7.92 millimetre calibre, what is the effective range of this type of weapon?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Maximum range is 1200 metres, 1.2 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Hypothetically speaking, what would be the range of a higher calibre weapon, say of a heavy machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: A 50 calibre machine-gun or a 14.5 millimetre machine-gun would go out to 2.000 metres but this was not fire. And you have to look at the trajectory, the actual angle of fire in the actual videotape. The fire is actually going upwards, it's not going downwards so I mean -- but it was definitely 7.92 and it was not a heavy calibre machine-gun. A heavy calibre machine-gun has a different sound to it as opposed to a crack crack crack crack crack as we heard in the videotape, it will go boom boom boom boom boom. That's what a heavy calibre machine-gun does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. For the transcript, Mr. President, the witness, when he was talking about the crack crack crack very quickly, and the -- when he was talking about boom boom boom, he would slow down considerably. You spoke about the angle of the firing. What did you notice that you can tell us about in relation to the situation of the building, the position of the building and the positions and the enemy positions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: In terms of the position of the building, it was -- you could quite clearly see that on the narrow facade. There were tank shell holes from Serb tank fire accepted, but the actual fire that we saw in the videotape was coming from the east and it was coming from a weapon that was well outside any Serb weapon that was in -- to the east of Sarajevo not even on the map. I mean I can produce another map but the position was over here in terms of this map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to have to interrupt you by asking you the following question: Since you've told us that the Serb positions were in any case outside of this map, I'm going to ask you the following question: What was the calibre used?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given that the Defence counsel has chosen to ask questions about directions of fire by reference to the map, it would be appropriate for the Defence counsel to have the witness mark on the map the position of the building because without that, the questioning doesn't really have much value.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I disagree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's just try to practically the way it's done until now is not sufficient to have good records so would you please take the necessary measures either by describing what he points at or what he says or by having him to mark it. Marking is, as you might have noticed, the way preferred by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is how we'll proceed, Witness, could you please indicate -- but first I'm just going to check that we have the good map. Can you please zoom so that we can have the whole map? Thank you. Yes. Witness, could you please indicate if you can see it, from which locations more or less in your opinion the photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was taken from over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The witness points to the south of a road which is called the transit road -- which we have called the transit road. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the picture isn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... And I'll try to describe where the witness points at. Could the map be zoomed in a little bit? Mr. Gray, could you again point at the situation where, in your view, the picture was taken from.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: From here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness is pointing at a yellow road just north of it reads in Mrakusa and he points at the yellow road in that part of the map between the two blue lines where it reads Muslimana. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've had some audio problems, I don't know whether everyone has had the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have, as a matter of fact --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will proceed with only one microphone. I have no interpretation but never mind, I will base myself on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, witness, thank you. Looking at the map that you have before you, could you please indicate where are the buildings located that you have spoken about that is -- that you have pointed to already, that is the Holiday Inn building and the building next to it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They're in here, just in here. It's about -- it's a matter of the range question that really counts here, I mean, that really matters. The fact is that the Holiday Inn is in that area there, okay, and the nearest --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness's microphone be approached, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would be grateful if we could have a recording of the position indicated by the witness before we move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness was pointing at an area which is just north of the river, from Miljacka from where he earlier pointed the photo was taken -- that's north from Mrakusa on the map and that is a part that has been referred to many times as the old city.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that we can locate things, could you please point to the Marsal Tito barracks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness does so and he points his pointer on a rectangular structure and we know that this corresponds to the Marsal Tito barracks. Now, according to your recollection, what was the distance between the Marsal Tito barracks and the Holiday Inn Hotel?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I didn't actually sort of have the time or the effort or the -- to actually measure the actual distance but it was at least a kilometre away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, basing ourselves on the -- bearing in mind the scale of the map, would you care to reconsider your position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I presume we're talking about the firing on the building? The firing came from the east and Marsal Tito barracks is to the west.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
